title: Practice Passage 13: The Search for Liquid Water on Mars

passage.title: The Search for Liquid Water on Mars
passage.sub_title: Investigating ancient riverbeds, mineral deposits, subsurface ice lakes, and slope lineae on the Red Planet.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A

[A1] For decades, Mars has been the primary target for planetary scientists searching for extraterrestrial life. [A2] The planet is cold, dry, and has a very thin atmosphere, making the surface hostile to modern life forms. [A3] However, satellite images show features that resemble dried riverbeds and lake basins. [A4] These geological markings suggest that liquid water once flowed across the Martian surface in the ancient past.

Paragraph B

[B1] Liquid water is considered the most critical ingredient for life as we know it. [B2] On Earth, wherever liquid water is found, microbial life typically exists. [B3] Planetary scientists believe that if Mars once possessed liquid water, it may also have supported primitive microscopic organisms. [B4] Consequently, searching for signs of water has been the central goal of Martian exploration missions.

Paragraph C

[C1] Early robotic missions, such as the Viking landers in the 1970s, found no evidence of liquid water. [C2] The surface pressure on Mars is extremely low, meaning that liquid water would quickly evaporate or freeze. [C3] However, later rovers like Spirit and Opportunity discovered minerals that only form in the presence of water, such as hematite. [C4] These mineral discoveries confirmed that water must have persisted on Mars for long periods.

Paragraph D

[D1] In recent years, scientists have focused on the possibility of underground water. [D2] Satellite radar scans have detected reflections beneath the ice caps at the Martian poles. [D3] Some researchers believe these reflections indicate the presence of large lakes of liquid water sealed deep beneath the ice. [D4] However, other scientists argue that the radar reflections could be caused by clay minerals or volcanic rock.

Paragraph E

[E1] Another area of interest is the seasonal appearance of dark streaks on Martian slopes. [E2] These features, known as recurring slope lineae, appear during warm seasons and fade during colder months. [E3] Some experts suggest they are caused by flows of salty water, or brines, which have a lower freezing point than pure water. [E4] Nevertheless, other studies suggest the streaks may simply be dry flows of dust and sand.

Paragraph F

[F1] Analyzing Martian meteorites has also provided valuable clues. [F2] These are rocks that were blasted off the surface of Mars by asteroid impacts and eventually landed on Earth. [F3] Some meteorites contain tiny bubbles of water trapped inside their mineral structures. [F4] Testing these bubbles allows scientists to study the history and chemical composition of ancient Martian water directly.

Paragraph G

[G1] The search for Martian water continues with advanced rovers and planned sample-return missions. [G2] Scientists hope to bring rocks back to Earth where they can be analyzed in sophisticated laboratories. [G3] Determining whether Mars ever supported life remains one of the greatest scientific quests of our era. [G4] Finding even fossilized microbes would transform our understanding of our place in the universe.
